What is the OTU Pipeline?

The OTU (Operational Taxonomic Unit) pipeline clusters closely related 16S rRNA gene sequences together at 97% sequence similarity. Sequences that are 97% identical or higher are grouped into a single representative unit (an OTU). This is the classic, widely established approach for studying microbial communities.

Below is an explanation of each output file in this folder and how to use it.

1Primary Abundance Tables

Table
OTUs-Table.tab
What it is
A tab-separated text table containing the count (abundance) of each 97% OTU across all your samples. Rows represent OTU clusters, columns represent your sample IDs, and the final column shows the assigned taxonomy (Domain down to Species).
Use it for
This is the main data table for your downstream analysis. You can open it in Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, R (using packages like phyloseq, vegan, or DESeq2), Python, or statistical software to compare microbial composition, calculate diversity metrics, and identify differentially abundant bacteria between sample groups.
Table
SampleMinCount_Normalized-OTUs-Table.tab
What it is
The OTU abundance table normalized by subsampling (rarefying) every sample to match the sample with the lowest total read count.
Use it for
Fair comparison between samples. Because sequencing depth often varies between samples, this normalized table helps remove library-size bias before computing alpha and beta diversity.
Table
Spike_Normalized-OTUs-Table.tabPresent only if spike-ins were used
What it is
The OTU abundance table normalized against the internal spike-in DNA standards added to your samples before sequencing.
Use it for
Absolute quantification. While standard tables provide relative percentages, this table allows you to estimate absolute microbial loads (e.g., cell counts or copy numbers per gram of sample).

2Representative Sequences

Sequences
OTUs-Seqs.fasta
What it is
A standard FASTA file containing the representative (centroid) DNA sequence for each 97% OTU cluster. The header line for each sequence contains the OTU identifier and its assigned taxonomy.
Use it for
Inspecting the actual DNA sequences of your OTUs. Use this file for sequence alignments, BLAST searches against NCBI, designing targeted PCR primers, or constructing custom phylogenetic trees.

3Phylogenetic Trees

Tree
OTUs-Tree-nj.tre
What it is
A phylogenetic tree of the OTU representative sequences saved in standard Newick format (.tre), constructed using the Neighbor-Joining algorithm.
Use it for
Phylogeny-aware microbiome analyses, such as calculating UniFrac distances (weighted or unweighted) in QIIME 2 or phyloseq. You can also visualize this tree in interactive viewers like FigTree, iTOL, or Microreact.

4Interactive Visualizations

Interactive
OTUs-Krona.html
What it is
An interactive, visual taxonomy chart (Krona plot) that opens in any web browser.
Use it for
Exploring the bacterial composition of your samples visually without any coding. Simply double-click the file to open it in Chrome, Firefox, Safari, or Edge. You can click on the colored concentric rings to zoom in and out through Domain, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, and Species.

5SILVA 144+ Dual Outputs (*-8Levels.*)

Generated when a reference database with bacterial kingdoms is used, e.g. SILVA >= 144

Table
OTUs-Table-8Levels.tab
OTUs-Seqs-8Levels.fasta
OTUs-Krona-8Levels.html
SampleMinCount_Normalized-OTUs-Table-8Levels.tab
Spike_Normalized-OTUs-Table-8Levels.tabIf spike-ins were used
What they are
The exact same OTU results as above, but with 8 taxonomic ranks that explicitly include the bacterial Kingdom rank (e.g., Bacillati, Pseudomonadati, Fusobacteriati) between Domain and Phylum.
Use them for
Use the *-8Levels files if you need the latest SILVA 144+ kingdom classification (e.g., for Namco, Rhea, or Krona). Use the standard (7-level) files above if your downstream software (like PICRUSt2 or older R scripts) expects classic 7-level taxonomies.
